title: Ignatius to the Philadelphians
subtitle: one thanksgiving, one altar, one overseer, and a quarrel over the archives
lead: From Troas, on his way to die in Rome, Ignatius of Antioch writes back to the church at Philadelphia, where he had stayed on the road. He had found there 'not division' but 'filtering' (3:1): the church had strained out teachers who kept apart from its overseer. Now he warns it against anyone who 'interprets Judaism' (6:1), calls it to 'one thanksgiving', 'one altar' and 'one overseer' (4:1), and recalls the cry he made among them 'in a loud voice, the voice of God: "Pay attention to the overseer"' (7:1).

The letter holds the much-argued exchange about 'the archives': 'Unless I find it in the archives, I do not believe it in the gospel.' 'It is written.' 'That is the question.' 'But to me Jesus Christ is the archives' (8:2). No church counts the letter as Scripture; it is read here as an early witness, with the New Testament as the measure.
facts: No church. It is not in the New Testament of the Council of Trent (Catholic), the Westminster Confession (Reformed), the Second London Baptist Confession, the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's list of 35 New Testament books, or the Thirty-Nine Articles' 'Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received'.
Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, on his way to execution in Rome. Eusebius names the letter (Church History 3.36.10).

Written at Troas (11:2), with Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans and Ignatius to Polycarp, after the letters from Smyrna (Eusebius, Church History 3.36.5-10). Lake: Eusebius's Chronicle puts the martyrdom 'in the tenth year of Trajan, i.e. 108 A.D.', and there is 'a general tendency to think that Ignatius was really a martyr in Rome in the time of Trajan (98-117 A.D.)'.
Troas, on the coast of Asia, by Burrhus (11:2)
The church at Philadelphia in Asia, with its overseer, elders and deacons (1:0)
Letter of a condemned prisoner, against division and Judaizing teaching
Kirsopp Lake's Greek (Loeb, 1912), the short (middle) recension: the Medicean manuscript at Florence (G), the long recension (g), and the Latin (L), Armenian (A) and Syriac (S) versions.
authorship: The letter claims to be by 'Ignatius, also called Theophorus' (1:0), a prisoner (5:1; 7:2) writing from Troas (11:2) after a visit to Philadelphia (1:1; 3:1; 7:1). Eusebius names it among the seven letters: from Troas Ignatius 'again addressed in writing those in Philadelphia' (Church History 3.36.10, the site's translation of the Greek). Lightfoot finds in the obscure allusions of 7:1 'a strong testimony to the genuineness of the letter'.

The seven letters survive in three forms: a long recension of thirteen letters with interpolations, the short recension of the seven Eusebius names, and a Syriac abridgment of three that does not include Philadelphians (Lake). In 1910 the Catholic Encyclopedia judged that 'the best modern criticism favors the authenticity of the seven letters mentioned by Eusebius'. Later in the twentieth century the question was opened again. Sergio Zañartu's survey (Teología y Vida, 2009) names R. Weijenborg (1969), who argued that the short recension was made from the long one; R. Joly (1979), who held the letters a forgery written in Smyrna between 165 and 168; J. Rius-Camps (1980), who kept as genuine only the four letters written from Smyrna, so not this one; R. M. Hübner (1997), who dated the letters between 165 and 175; and T. Lechner (1999). Zañartu quotes W. R. Schoedel (1987), who expected the short recension to remain what 'the scholarly consensus today' sees in it, 'a collection of genuine letters of Bishop Ignatius of Antioch', and himself holds to its authenticity 'until the contrary is proved' (the site's translations of his Spanish). B. A. Zuiddam (Ekklesiastikos Pharos, 2010) argues that the seven-letter text may be a medieval abridgment. Lake follows the short recension.

audience.to: The church at Philadelphia, a city of Lydia in the Roman province of Asia, on the road from the Maeander valley to Sardis and Smyrna. Ignatius had passed through it under guard and met its overseer, whom he does not name (1:1). It had an overseer, a council of elders and deacons (1:0; 4:1; 7:1), and most of it was sound in his eyes: he found 'not division' but 'filtering' (3:1). Ignatius warns against anyone who 'interprets Judaism' (6:1) and recalls people who would believe nothing they could not find 'in the archives' (8:2). Lightfoot takes these to be one group of Gentile Christians urging Jewish practice from the prophets; the letter does not name them, and Lake says it is disputed whether such Judaizers were the docetists of the other letters. Some suspected Ignatius of having been briefed beforehand (7:2), and some dishonored his companions Philo and Rheus Agathopus (11:1).
audience.why: Lake gives the purpose of each letter except Romans as thanks for kindness shown, with three further motives: respect for the bishop and elders, protest against docetism and Judaistic practices, and help for the church at Antioch. All three are here: unity around the overseer and the one thanksgiving (1-4; 7-8), the warning against 'Judaism' and the answer about the archives (5-6; 8-9), and the request for an envoy to Antioch (10). Knowing that the letter answers a quarrel Ignatius himself had been part of explains its personal defense (6:3; 7:1-2) and the sharp exchange of 8:2.
views: Lightfoot calls the heresy 'a form of Docetic Judaism', attacked 'more directly from its Judaic than from its Docetic side', and thinks the teachers of 6:1 were 'Gentile Christians with strong Judaic tendencies'. Lake says 'it is disputed' whether the Judaizing tendency was 'found in docetic circles, or ... a danger threatening the church from other directions'. The Catholic Encyclopedia's article on the Docetae holds that in Ignatius's day 'Docetism seems to have been closely connected with Judaism', citing this letter's chapters 6 and 8.

outline: Greeting to the church in Philadelphia
Not the Father's planting; filtering, not division
One thanksgiving, one altar, one overseer
I cried out with God's voice
The priests, the high priest, the door of the Father
Philo and Rheus Agathopus; greetings from Troas

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Reads the letter as a source: Ignatius's visit to Philadelphia, who 'interprets Judaism' and argues from 'the archives', Philo and Rheus Agathopus, and the peace at Antioch.

lenses.name: New Testament
lenses.desc: Follows the New Testament in the letter: Galatians 1:1 and Philippians 2:3 in 1:1 and 8:2, Matthew 15:13 and 23:24 in 3:1, 1 Corinthians 6:9-10 and 10:16-17 in 3:3 and 4:1, John 3:8 in 7:1, Hebrews and John 10 in 9:1, and Revelation's letter to the same city (Revelation 3:7-13).

lenses.name: Church order and the churches
lenses.desc: Reads the letter for the questions churches still ask of it: one thanksgiving and one altar under one overseer (4:1), the overseer's call (1:0-1), prophecy in the assembly (7:1-2), Scripture, 'the archives' and the gospel (8:2), and churches sending overseers, elders and deacons (10:1-2).

sections.h: A visit, and a letter from Troas
sections.b: Unlike the churches of Magnesia and Tralles, Philadelphia had been visited by Ignatius himself (Lightfoot). 'I know' (1:1), 'I found' (3:1), 'I cried out while I was among you' (7:1) and 'I was a burden to no one' (6:3) look back to that stay. The letter was written later from Troas (11:2), where Philo and Rheus Agathopus caught up with him, bringing news that the church at Antioch was at peace (10:1; Lightfoot) and that some at Philadelphia had dishonored them (11:1).

sections.h: One thanksgiving, one altar, one overseer
sections.b: The heart of Ignatius's answer to division is 4:1: 'one thanksgiving', 'one flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ', 'one cup', 'one altar', 'one overseer'. The words build on 1 Corinthians 10:16-17. The Spirit's message at Philadelphia was the same: 'Do nothing without the overseer' (7:2). Lightfoot thinks the stress on 'one' answers a rival meal. The views note at 4:1 gives how the verse is read; the cards on the Supper at John 6, Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 8 and Acts 20:7 set out the churches' answers.

Ignatius warns against anyone who 'interprets Judaism' (6:1), and he recalls a debate: some would believe nothing in the gospel they could not find 'in the archives'; when he said 'It is written', they answered 'That is the question'; and he replied that 'to me Jesus Christ is the archives' (8:2). Lake and Lightfoot take 'the archives' as the Old Testament. The words are about teachers in the church, and the letter honors the prophets (5:2) and the priests (9:1). On how such passages were later used against Jews, see the topic on anti-Judaism; on the debate itself, the deep notes at chapters 6 and 8.

Ignatius loves the prophets, who 'pointed to the gospel' and were saved by believing in Christ (5:2); they came to the Father through Christ, 'the Father's door', with the patriarchs, the apostles and the church (9:1). Yet 'the gospel has something special: the coming of the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, his suffering and the resurrection' (9:2). Whether 'the gospel' and 'the apostles' (5:1) are already written books is argued; Lightfoot leans toward the message.

Each of the three letters from Troas asks for an envoy to Antioch (10:1; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 11:2; Ignatius to Polycarp 7:2). Here the church is to 'elect a deacon'; other churches have sent overseers, elders and deacons (10:2). Lake counts this among Ignatius's motives: 'to secure the future of his own church in Antioch by persuading other communities to send helpers'.

spec.title: Claude's theory: two letters to one church
spec.body: Revelation's letter to Philadelphia promises an 'open door' (Revelation 3:8), names 'the synagogue of Satan, who say they are Jews and are not' (Revelation 3:9), and promises the faithful a place 'in the temple of my God' (Revelation 3:12). Ignatius's letter to the same church calls Christ 'the Father's door' (9:1), warns against those who 'interpret Judaism' (6:1), and speaks of the high priest and the most holy place (9:1). Lightfoot notices the door. I suggest that the Philadelphian church may have treasured the Revelation letter, so that Ignatius's pictures of door and temple would have sounded familiar to its members. This is my suggestion; Ignatius never quotes Revelation, and the two letters may simply share the city's situation.

prompts: I cried out with God's voice (7:1)

In a modest hall in a hillside town among vineyards, a bearded prisoner in chains, flanked by bored Roman soldiers, stands and calls out with lifted hand; an older quiet overseer sits with elders around him, and some listeners lean in while others whisper behind their hands.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, Egyptian hieroglyphic register lines and small glyph borders, plus a few bold flat shapes of lapis blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. Wide horizontal composition, 3:2.
To me Jesus Christ is the archives (8:2)

A small group of men argue over open scrolls taken from wooden cubbyholes of an ancient record room; across from them the chained prisoner points not at the scrolls but upward to a faint cross with an empty tomb behind it.

canon.summary: Ignatius to the Philadelphians is an early Christian letter in no church's Bible. Its author, the martyr Ignatius of Antioch, is honored as a saint by Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches.
accepted_by: Not Scripture: the Council of Trent's list of New Testament books (1546) does not include it. The U.S. bishops' Liturgical Calendar for 2026 keeps 17 October as the Memorial of 'Saint Ignatius of Antioch, Bishop and Martyr'. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) lists this letter's chapter 3 among its witnesses to the church as 'a visible society' and to 'the unity of the Church'.

Not part of the Bible, in the words of George Reid, writing in the Catholic Encyclopedia (1908): the Eastern Orthodox churches 'have a New Testament identical with the Catholic'. The Orthodox Church in America commemorates 'Hieromartyr Ignatius the God-Bearer, Bishop of Antioch' on 20 December; its life of him says he 'wrote seven epistles: to the churches of Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles, Rome, Philadelphia, and Smyrna'.
Not Scripture: the church's list of 35 New Testament books, which adds eight books to the 27, among them 'The book of Clement' and the 'Didascalia', does not name it.

Not Scripture: Article VI receives 'All the Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received'. The Church of England's Common Worship calendar keeps 17 October as a Lesser Festival of 'Ignatius, Bishop of Antioch, Martyr, c.107'.

The calendar of the synod's Southern District commemorates 'Ignatius of Antioch, Pastor and Martyr' on 17 October, and its page names this church among those he wrote to, at 'Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles, Rome, Philadelphia, and Smyrna'. That is a district page; the synod's own calendar was not opened.
Not Scripture: the Westminster Confession lists the 27 books of the New Testament as 'all the books of the Old and New Testaments, which are these'.
Not Scripture: the Second London Baptist Confession (1689) lists the same 27 books, 'All of which are given by the inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life'.

provenance.b: Ignatius had passed through Philadelphia on his way to Smyrna (Lightfoot; 1:1; 7:1). From Troas, Eusebius says, he 'again addressed in writing those in Philadelphia' (Church History 3.36.10). Burrhus, the Ephesian deacon, wrote or carried it (11:2).

In the Greek Medicean manuscript at Florence (G) with the other short-recension letters except Romans; in the interpolated long recension (g); in the Latin version Robert Grosseteste made in 1250 (L); and in Armenian and Syriac versions (A, S) (Lake). The Syriac abridgment of three letters found by Cureton in 1845 does not include it.

rejected_why.h: A bishop's letter, not an apostle's
rejected_why.b: The early church received into the New Testament writings it held to come from the apostles and their circle. Ignatius sets himself below the apostles: 'They were apostles; I am a condemned man' (Ignatius to the Romans 4:3). In this letter he takes refuge 'in the apostles as in the church's council of elders' (5:1), as one who looks to them.

rejected_why.h: Treated as a letter of a church writer
rejected_why.b: Eusebius names the letter in his history (Church History 3.36.10) and does not mention Ignatius in his survey of the books accepted, disputed and rejected for the New Testament (Church History 3.25).

cited_in.b: Both writings are addressed to the church at Philadelphia. Revelation speaks of 'an open door' and of 'those who say they are Jews and are not' (Revelation 3:8-9); Ignatius calls Christ 'the Father's door' (9:1) and warns against those who 'interpret Judaism' (6:1). Lightfoot notes the door; any link between the two opponents is an inference. The New Testament does not quote this letter.
Ignatius takes up John's words about the Spirit, 'where it comes from and where it is going'; Lightfoot holds the Gospel 'prior' and the agreement 'quite too strong to be accidental'.
The overseer's ministry came 'not from himself or through human beings', Lightfoot's 'obvious reflexion' of Paul's 'not from people, and not through any human being'.
One cup, one loaf, one body: Lake's margin sets Paul's words beside the 'one thanksgiving' of 4:1.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to Christian life early in the second century the letter is of great value: it shows a church in Asia with one overseer, elders and deacons, a single shared thanksgiving of bread and cup, prophetic speech in the gathering, and a live debate about how the Jewish Scriptures relate to the gospel. Its text rests on one Greek manuscript of the short recension with the versions and the long recension. Its few historical claims fit Eusebius. In doctrine it follows the New Testament on Christ; its rule that all must be done with the overseer goes beyond what the New Testament says.

sections.h: 1. As a witness to early Christian belief
sections.b: High. The letter shows how one church leader, a generation or two after the apostles, met division: by the one thanksgiving (4:1), the overseer with his elders and deacons (1:0; 7:1-2), and Christ's cross and resurrection as the measure of the Scriptures (8:2). It shows Christians honoring the prophets and the priests of Israel while placing Christ above them (5:2; 9:1-2), and churches sending delegates to one another (10:1-2).

The short recension survives in Greek in one manuscript, the Medicean at Florence (G), published by Vossius in 1646; Lake also uses the long recension (g), Grosseteste's Latin (L), and the Armenian (A), made from a lost Syriac version (Lake). G has slips that the others correct: it drops 'God's voice' at 7:1, reads 'snatched away' for 'incomplete' at 5:1 and 'the ancient (writings)' for 'the archives' at 8:2 (Lightfoot's apparatus). Lake prints the readings of the other witnesses there; the variants give both.

The letter claims to be by Ignatius, writing from Troas after a stay at Philadelphia (11:2; 7:1), and tells of peace restored at Antioch (10:1). Eusebius knew it as his (Church History 3.36.10). The debate over the genuineness of the seven letters is in the authorship section; Rius-Camps (1980), as Zañartu reports him, kept as genuine only the letters written from Smyrna, so not this one.

Matches: the one cup and one loaf (4:1; 1 Corinthians 10:16-17); a ministry 'not from himself or through human beings' (1:1; Galatians 1:1); the Spirit who knows its way and exposes secrets (7:1; John 3:8; 1 Corinthians 2:10); the body as God's temple (7:2; 1 Corinthians 6:19); Christ the high priest and the door (9:1; Hebrews 9:7-12; John 10:9); the prophets who looked ahead to Christ (5:2; 1 Peter 1:10-12). Goes beyond: 'Do nothing without the overseer' (7:2) and the joining of one altar to one overseer (4:1) have no parallel in the New Testament, where elders and overseers seem to be the same leaders (Acts 20:17, 28; Titus 1:5-7); churches read this difference differently (see the cards at Acts 20:28, Philippians 1:1 and 1 Timothy 3). Conflicts: none on a point of doctrine.

how_to_read.h: As one side of a conversation
how_to_read.b: Ignatius answers people he had met and argued with. Read 6:3-8:2 as his account of a visit that went partly wrong, and 3:1 as his praise of the church for coming through it.

The exchange about 'the archives' is short and easily misread. Read it with the note and the deep notes at chapter 8, which give the punctuation Lightfoot argues for and the Plain English Translation follows, the common reading Lake prefers, and Zahn's.

how_to_read.h: As a witness the churches read differently
how_to_read.b: Catholic writers cite the letter for the unity of the church and the Eucharist (the Catholic Encyclopedia on chapter 3 and Pohle on chapter 4). The notes point to the cards on the 66 books where the churches set out their teaching.
